title: Supporting the falling
hook: God supports the falling, heals the sick, frees the bound

segments.voice: Yesterday, Avot, the blessing that opens with a family. Your line was god of our fathers and mothers. Did you tell one ancestor's story? Today, the second blessing, and a surprising definition of strength. Day five hundred seventy-eight.

Ask a room of ten-year-olds what makes someone strong. You'll hear about lifting cars, winning fights, never crying. Ask the same question at a nursing home and you'll hear something else entirely. The nurse who came at three in the morning. The neighbor who drove someone to dialysis twice a week for a year. The second blessing of the Amidah is about God's strength. And when it lists what that strength actually does, there isn't a single battle in it.
screen: `WHAT MAKES SOMEONE STRONG?` → `THE NURSE AT THREE IN THE MORNING.` → `NOT A SINGLE BATTLE.`

segments.voice: The blessing is called Gevurot: powers, mighty deeds. From gibor, a hero, a mighty one. It begins: You are mighty forever. And then it says what the might is for. Sustaining the living with kindness. Supporting the falling. Healing the sick. Freeing the bound. Keeping faith with those who sleep in the dust. Those phrases come from the Psalms. In the old Jewish translation, Psalm 145 says: "The LORD upholdeth all that fall, and raiseth up all those that are bowed down." Psalm 146 adds that the Lord looses the prisoners and opens the eyes of the blind. So the blessing defines power as the power to catch. The traditional text also says, more than once, that God gives life to the dead, and it closes with those words: blessed are You, who revives the dead. Resurrection is a classical Jewish belief, one of Maimonides' thirteen principles. Many Reform prayer books instead say who gives life to all, and some offer both; Orthodox and many Conservative communities keep the traditional ending. There's a further step the rabbis take. In the Talmud, Sotah 14a, they ask how a person can walk after God, and answer: follow God's ways. As God clothed the naked and visited the sick, so you. Read the blessing that way and it becomes a job list. The might described here is something human hands can practice. Support the falling is a sentence about God. It's also a set of instructions.
screen: `GEVUROT: POWERS, MIGHTY DEEDS.` · `SUPPORT, HEAL, FREE.` · `WHO REVIVES THE DEAD, OR GIVES LIFE TO ALL.` · `WALK IN GOD'S WAYS.` · then, large: `SUPPORT THE FALLING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: support someone who's falling. Settle, and breathe. Think of the people in your life this month. Who's slipping? Someone short of money, short of sleep, short of hope. Someone who's gone quiet in the group chat. Pick one face. Now picture one concrete way to put a hand under them: a call, a meal, a ride, an hour of your time, a sentence that says I noticed. Keep it small enough to actually do today. The bell holds the time.
Gevurot. Powers, mighty deeds. The Amidah's second blessing, where strength means supporting the falling, healing the sick and freeing the bound.
Your line: support the falling. Today, do the small thing you pictured for the person who's slipping, before the day gets away from you. Day five hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Gevurot is the second blessing of every Amidah; the traditional text praises God who revives the dead, while many Reform prayer books say who gives life to all, and many teachers read its list of deeds as a model for human action.

myth: the blessing of God's might is mostly about battles
it lists sustaining, supporting, healing and freeing: power used to catch.
every Jewish prayer book ends this blessing the same way
the traditional text says who revives the dead; many Reform books say who gives life to all.
the Talmud teaches imitating God's acts of care

fork.setup: the rabbis read that a person should walk after God. how, they ask, can anyone walk after God?
options: by following God's ways: clothing, visiting, comforting.
fork.reveal: Sotah 14a: follow God's attributes. as God clothed the naked and visited the sick, so you.

original.note: Hebrew: supporting the falling. a phrase of the Amidah's second blessing, echoing Psalm 145:14.

trapdoor: what you thought: a blessing praising how powerful God is.
what it means: power defined as catching: supporting the falling, healing, freeing, keeping faith.
what a scholar hears: Psalm 145:14 and 146:7–8 behind the phrases; resurrection as a classical principle (Maimonides' thirteenth), with mechayeh hakol in many Reform books.
